title: From Roe to Reagan: The Framing of Abortion in Congressional Hearings and the Development of Issue Positions
abstract: This thesis examines how moral, feminist, and medical frames have shaped the issue positions of the Democratic and Republican parties between 1973, following the Roe v. Wade decision, and 1989, through the Reagan administration. Drawing on congressional hearing transcripts and presidential documents, this inquiry uses Carmines and Stimson’s issue evolution model, along with Chong and Druckman’s framing theory, to argue that language at the elite level actively constructed the partisan divide over abortion. An analysis of this evidence illustrates the early dominance of the moral frame, followed by medical and feminist framing in a congressional setting that prioritized legitimacy. However, presidential remarks, used for the purpose of mobilization, translated elite debates to the public without the use of complex medical terminology. Taken together, these findings reveal how the abortion framing seen today originated at the congressional level, resulting in consequences for women’s health and reproductive rights.

title: “Americans aren’t serfs.” Institutional Investors, Nationalized Politics, and Congressional Housing Rhetoric
abstract: Institutional investors have purchased millions of single-family homes across the United States, concentrating ownership in Sunbelt and major metropolitan markets and generating significant public and political concern. Yet no research focuses on whether representatives respond to this structural transformation of local housing markets through political rhetoric. This thesis answers the question: do U.S. House representatives from districts with high institutional investor penetration adopt more housing rhetoric in congressional floor speeches? Using a dataset of 851 representative-Congress observations spanning the 117th and 118th Congresses and nine model specifications, I find that investor penetration does not predict corporate landlord, supply and zoning, or affordability rhetoric. Instead, median gross rent is a primary predictor of housing rhetoric, and Republicans discuss housing affordability significantly less than Democrats, suggesting representatives respond to visible cost conditions and partisan identity rather than local ownership structure. Four case studies illuminate the mechanisms behind the null on investor penetration, showing that policy entrepreneurship, committee position, and partisan ideology can drive housing rhetoric independently of local conditions. Even districts with among the highest penetration in the sample produce complete rhetorical silence when those channels are absent.

title: The Politics of Uncertainty: Information and the Making of Learned Political Helplessness in Lebanon
abstract: Why does Lebanon’s political system remain resilient despite recurring crises, economic collapse, and widespread public disillusionment? Existing explanations emphasize sectarianism and clientelism, which account for elite endurance but do not explain how citizens come to believe that political change is impossible. I argue that Lebanese citizens’ perception of the information environment as fragmented, politicized, and crisis-normalizing plays a central role in producing what I call learned political helplessness—a cognitive expectation that political action will not alter outcomes. State opacity and partisan media generate confusion, distrust, and contradictory narratives, leading citizens to repeatedly witness failed reform efforts and normalize dysfunction. These dynamics erode citizens’ sense of both internal and external political efficacy and help explain why widespread frustration rarely translates into sustained collective action demanding change, thereby enabling the political system’s continuation. The October 2019 uprising serves as a powerful exception to the rule of learned political helplessness that helps us understand the mechanisms that typically underlie the absence of collective action challenging the political status quo. It was a brief moment when decentralized, cross-sectarian information networks appear to have temporarily altered citizens’ perceptions of the otherwise fragmented and politicized information environment by enabling the rapid circulation of shared narratives about corruption, accountability, and collective grievance outside elite-controlled media channels, and thereby, reactivated citizens’ belief that coordinated political action could meaningfully challenge the political status quo. Its rapid rise and collapse provide analytical leverage for tracing how shifts in information shape expectations of political possibility. Specifically, it helps explain how temporary informational coherence in the perceived information environment can reduce perceived barriers to action, and how its fragmentation rapidly reinstates expectations of political futility. To demonstrate how the perceived information environment produces and reinforces learned political helplessness, thereby stabilizing political continuity despite grievance, this study employs a multi-method within-case research design integrating qualitative content analysis of state and media outputs, process tracing of the 2019 uprising, semi-structured interviews, and an original nationally representative survey with an embedded experiment. This design allows the study to trace causal mechanisms linking perceptions of information exposure to political expectations while holding constant structural factors such as sectarian identity, repression, and economic hardship. The empirical findings provide partial support for the proposed mechanism linking perceptions of the information environment—particularly perceptions of crisis-normalizing narratives communicated through partisan media and political elites—to higher levels of cognitive learned political helplessness. Perceptions of the information environment—particularly crisis-normalizing narratives—are significantly associated with higher levels of cognitive learned political helplessness, although helplessness itself does not significantly predict willingness to engage in collective action. Taken together, the findings suggest that while the perceived information environment contributes to the internalization of political futility—by associating crisis-normalizing narratives with higher levels of cognitive learned political helplessness—this helplessness alone does not translate into greater or lower willingness to engage in collective action. The results therefore provide support for the informational mechanism shaping expectations of political possibility, while indicating that additional factors beyond cognitive helplessness likely shape whether grievances ultimately produce collective mobilization challenging the political status quo. Overall, the thesis advances a new lens for understanding political continuity in Lebanon: systems may persist not only through institutions and elite strategies, but through the internalization of powerlessness among the publics they govern.

title: East Asian Pathways To Democracy Through External Democratizing Pressure: A Qualitative Comparative Analysis
abstract: This thesis examines the interplay between external pressure and domestic conditions in the democratization of East and Southeast Asian states between 1980 and 2000. While the region experienced rapid economic growth during the late twentieth century, regime outcomes diverged significantly. As some states transitioned to democracy, others sustained durable authoritarian rule. Existing scholarship has often emphasized either structural modernization or external Western pressure but has paid insufficient attention to how these forces interact within the distinct historical and geopolitical context of East Asia. Building on the framework of linkage and leverage developed by Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way, this study investigates how domestic factors – including organizational power, economic development, and mass contention – condition external pressures (e.g., sanctions, aid conditionality, and integration into Western economic and cultural networks). Using crisp-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (csQCA) across fourteen cases, the study identifies multiple equifinal pathways to both democratization and authoritarian resilience. The findings reveal that external pressure alone is insufficient to produce democratic transitions. Instead, democratization occurs through distinct causal configurations: modernization-driven pathways in states with high levels of economic development and Western linkage, domestically driven pathways where sustained mass contention compensates for weak external ties, and externally driven pathways where strong linkage and leverage interact with less favorable domestic conditions. Conversely, authoritarian resilience can persist in configurations characterized by high economic development, weak organizational power, and mass contention. By highlighting the conditional nature of democratization, this study demonstrates that regime outcomes in East Asia are shaped not by single causal factors but by the interaction between external pressures and domestic political conditions. These findings contribute to broader debates in comparative politics by refining theories of democratization and underscoring the limits of external influence in the absence of favorable domestic conditions.

title: Faith, Finance, & Political Change: Islamic Banking and Context-Dependent Development Across the Global South
abstract: Islamic finance has grown into a multi-trillion-dollar global industry over the past few decades, shaping financial systems across both Muslim-majority and non-Muslim countries. Rooted in Shari’ah principles that prohibit interest (ribā) and emphasize risk-sharing, ethical investment, and social justice, Islamic banking is frequently presented as a transformative alternative to conventional financial systems. Amanah Advisors, a global Islamic finance advisory firm, argues that “Islam seeks to bring order and remove chaos, and Islamic Finance is there to bring order to chaos in the economy, markets and society” (Amanah Advisors; n.d. [accessed May 1, 2026]). Proponents similarly argue that these features promote economic inclusivity, reduce inequality, and contribute to broader socio-political stability. Yet despite these claims, there remains limited systematic evidence evaluating whether Islamic banking consistently delivers on these promises across diverse political and institutional contexts. While some case studies highlight potential benefits, other examples point to shortcomings, including the replication of conventional debt-like structures, limited risk-sharing in practice, and uneven access to financial services across populations. This thesis therefore examines the extent to which Islamic banks achieve their stated objectives, particularly in shaping socio-political and developmental outcomes. The motivation for this project is informed not only by these broader debates, but also by a gap in academic exposure and empirical clarity. The persistence of practices that mirror conventional finance, alongside mixed developmental outcomes in countries with significant Islamic banking sectors– particularly the Gulf countries–highlights a fundamental tension between the theoretical ideals and real-world implementation of Islamic finance.

title: Why Did the 2014 and 2022 Sanctions Targeting Russian Oligarchs Fail to Achieve Their Intended Political Objectives?
abstract: Western sanctions against Russian oligarchs were built on a flawed reading of who actually holds usable political leverage in Putin’s Russia. Using an intrinsic explanatory case study of Russia, the thesis combines elite interviews with Western policymakers, analysts, and one senior representative of a Russian oligarch, as well as document analysis and secondary literature to reconstruct how oligarch sanctions were supposed to work and how plausible that mechanism was given Russia’s regime structures. It shows that Western officials imagined a relatively linear chain running from financial pressure on oligarchs to oligarchs’ pressure on Putin and resulting constraints on Russia’s ability to wage war in Ukraine. Yet the political realities of a sultanistic oligarchy – centralized decision-making, oligarch dependence on the Kremlin, coercive measures and extensive adaptation and evasion strategies – meant that this chain was never likely to hold. By tracing the mismatch between imagined and actual levers of influence, the thesis explains the limited impact of sanctions focused on oligarchs and offers more cautious expectations for using similar tools against authoritarian regimes.

title: Stay In Your Lane?: How Media Narratives Approximate Factional Demand in Presidential Primaries
abstract: Presidential primaries are often described using the language of “lanes,” yet it is unclear what these categories represent. This thesis treats political lanes as media-constructed classificatory devices and asks whether they plausibly reflect underlying voter preferences. It analyzes a corpus of news coverage from the 2016 Republican and 2020 Democratic primaries alongside survey data from the American National Election Studies. Media texts are coded to identify recurring lane narratives, while voter preferences are mapped using clustering techniques. The findings show that ideological lanes align most closely with voter structure, while strategic lanes such as “establishment” or “electability” correspond weakly. Lane narratives are most prolific when elite coordination is weak and consolidate as coordination emerges. These patterns suggest that lanes may not always reflect voter demands, but they are narrative tools that vary in accuracy across contexts. The project clarifies how parties, media, and voters interpret competition under uncertainty.

title: When Americans Are Taken: Comparing U.S. Responses to State and Non-State Hostage Takers
abstract: This study aimed to examine how the type of perpetrator (state vs. non-state) taking an American hostage influences or alters the response from the U.S. government. Using a mixed methods approach including a small-N dataset coded from publicly available information, case study process tracing, and a survey analysis, this study found substantial support for the U.S. responding differently between state and non-state actors. The United States is more likely to engage in negotiations and offer concessions in cases involving state actors, while responses to non-state actors rely more heavily on coercive tools and exhibit greater variability. These differences are explained in part by varying credibility, legitimacy, and information asymmetry across perpetrator types. While public support for negotiation remains consistently high, attitudes toward concessions and coercive measures vary more, providing partial support for the relationship in public policy preferences and actor type. Despite the study’s limitations, the findings contribute to existing literature by demonstrating how the U.S. response differs, exploring how legitimacy and credibility shape U.S. decision-making processes, and offering a foundation for future research on hostage negotiation. Additionally, this study provides a step towards the fusion of terrorist studies with state-to-state scholarship in political science.

title: To Nuke, or Not To Nuke: How Leaders’ Dispositions Influence Major Nuclear Decisions
abstract: Why do some elite leaders acquire, test, or use nuclear weapons despite their costly effects, and why do other leaders not despite having the capability to do so? Current literature attributes leaders’ decisions to external factors, which explain the strategic motivations behind these leaders’ nuclear decisions. However, less is said about the role of disposition, or personality traits, and how they manifest into decisions that benefit the leader’s image but impose irreversible costs on the greater public. This thesis aims to study whether dispositional factors (narcissism and self-esteem) influence elite leaders’ nuclear decisions. I use process tracing analysis to conduct a three-way comparative case study consisting of Kim Jong-il (North Korea), Harry Truman (U.S.), and Eisaku Satō (Japan). Kim and Truman serve as positive cases (leaders who pursued major costly and/or escalatory decisions), while Satō will be my negative case (leaders who did not pursue major costly and/or escalatory decisions). I find that leaders who developed high narcissistic traits during childhood are more likely to pursue major escalatory nuclear decisions than leaders who developed low narcissistic traits during childhood. I also find that low self-esteem amplifies the effect of narcissism on a leader’s nuclear decision by increasing their need for validation. Finally, I find that when dispositions inconsistently appear across a leader’s life, situational factors may be a stronger explanation for their nuclear decision, especially when the situational pressure is high. Overall, my thesis argues that while disposition may be a contributing factor, it does not fully determine leaders’ decision to pursue major escalatory nuclear decisions.

advisor: Daniel C. Molden (Psychology) and Alexander Coppock
title: The Role of Elite Cues and Endorsements of Political Violence in Shaping Individual Attitudes
abstract: Recent acts of partisan-driven violence have raised questions about the extent to which individuals are willing to support these behaviors, especially when encouraged to do so by elected officials. Given the low support for extreme political violence (Holliday, Lelkes, and Westwood 2024; Kalmoe and Mason 2022), the current study focuses on less extreme forms and their attitudinal precursors, such as hostility linked to perceptions of dehumanization in partisan polarization. Previous research has also shown that meta-perceptions of support for political violence are a key mediator in shaping the relationship between exposure to violent rhetoric and individual-level attitudes toward political violence (Mernyk et al. 2022). Consequently, this study uses a survey experiment to examine how rhetoric from a Republican elite endorsing political violence affect broader perceptions of and individual-level support for political violence (SPV). An initial pilot study (N = 300) sampling only Republicans reported a null average treatment effect across all measured outcome variables, except for affective evaluations of the Republican Party—that of the speaker. Subsequently, the treatment produced no significant effect among Republican participants within the main study (N = 790), consistent with the conclusion that in-party elite cues have a null effect on the predicted outcomes. However, examinations of group-specific effects identified a significant treatment effect on meta-perceptions of the average Republican’s SPV and individual SPV among weaker-identifying Democrats. This suggests an alternative unanticipated hypothesis that runs contrary to our initial hypotheses, wherein partisan identity may moderate responsiveness to elite rhetoric through pathways otherwise neglected according to the standard framework.

title: Ideological Expectations: How Candidate Conservatism Shapes Voter Preferences for Women in U.S. Executive Elections
abstract: While women US presidential nominees have only been seen in the Democratic party, punditry predicts the first woman president will be a Republican (Campbell and Lovenduski 2025; Simon 2024; Winter 2010). Similarly, in international politics links can be drawn between conservatism and electoral success for women executive candidates (Worthy et al. 2023). I dissect the interaction between conservatism and willingness to vote for women US executive candidates through two investigations. I conduct a historical study of this relationship using content analysis to provide an ideological score for US women governors since 1964. Regressing ideological score on female vote share provides preliminary evidence to suggest there is a positive correlation between conservatism and female vote share. Then, I conduct a vignette survey experiment to test whether voters are more likely to vote for a more conservative female presidential candidate compared to a less conservative counterpart. Greater conservatism is associated with a decreased likelihood of voting for a candidate among Democrats; the opposite is true of Republicans. The study highlights that more conservative women candidates are seen as more traditional and masculine. The results reveal that Democrats are less likely to vote for the more conservative party nominee compared to their less conservative counterpart, while Republicans are more likely to vote for the more conservative party nominee or are approximately indifferent between the two. However, when information is given about the level of traditionality and masculinity, these responses change. Democrats’ likelihood of voting for the more conservative candidate increases when they are portrayed as less traditional or less masculine; the reverse is true of Republicans. Taken together, these studies provide preliminary support to suggest that elements of perceived conservatism impact willingness to vote for women executive candidates; this effect differs between parties.

title: How does rights-based climate litigation impact environmental policy outcomes?: Evidence from Colombia and Nepal
abstract: In the last decade, lawsuits invoking the constitutional right to a healthy environment have proliferated as a strategy to spur government action on climate change. Yet their effectiveness in shaping environmental policy remains unclear. This study therefore poses the question: how does successful climate litigation based on the right to a healthy environment ultimately affect environmental policy outcomes? I focus on two hypothesized causal mechanisms: the specificity of court orders and civil society pressures. To test these hypotheses, I conduct a qualitative case study of two successful rights-based climate lawsuits, one in Colombia and one in Nepal. I draw upon legal materials, government documents, and media coverage to process trace the links between litigation and policy change. I find that clear and actionable court orders, as well as sustained civil society advocacy, play an important role in driving environmental policy progress. However, courts are ultimately the most crucial actors ensuring post-ruling policy change. Overall, this study illuminates the conditions under which rights-based climate litigation is a productive strategy for motivating government action in the face of escalating climate threats.

title: Recognition without Responsiveness: Comparing the Turkish-Armenian and Armenian-American Communities
abstract: This thesis examines how classificatory systems shape political possibilities for ethnic minorities by comparing Armenian minorities in the United States and Turkey. Drawing on constructivist theories put forth by Rogers Brubaker, Ian Hacking, and Michel Foucault, this project analyzes how distinct regimes – American multiculturalism and Turkish nationalism – produce convergent outcomes of political marginalization for the Armenian ethnic community. This comparative study is based on 14 semi-structured interviews with American-Armenians conducted over Zoom with participants from across the U.S. and 14 interviews with Turkish-Armenians conducted in-person in Istanbul. Interviews were supplemented with ethnographic observations, secondary sources in Armenian studies, and archival research. In the U.S., Armenian-American legal classification as “white” enabled integration and institutional success for early Armenian immigrants, but renders current Armenian-American foreign policy claims as narrow ethnic interest demands. This limits policy success beyond symbolic recognition. In Turkey, Armenians are officially recognized as a religious minority under the Treaty of Lausanne, allowing for institutions to remain alive and functioning. However, suppression of ethnic identity and the criminalization of genocide discourse constrain open political advocacy. Across both contexts, recognition operates less as a form of political responsiveness than as a mechanism that limits political voice. These findings challenge the assumption that recognition leads to accountability, showing that classificatory regimes can shape whether states aptly respond to the minority communities they claim to represent.

title: A Troubling Refrain: The Impact of the Northern Irish Troubles on Far-Right Ideology in the Republic of Ireland
abstract: As seen by the anti-immigration riots which ripped through Dublin in November 2023, far-right xenophobic sentiments have infiltrated the Republic of Ireland, a nation long-thought to be an outlier in this global trend. While existing scholarship often treats contemporary Irish xenophobia as a recent phenomenon, this study explores whether and how the political and social impacts of the Troubles may contribute to its emergence. This thesis involves the analysis of ten interviews with Dublin City Councillors conducted in 2024, utilizing a qualitative, interpretive methodology of thematic analysis and process tracing. Analysis shows that the Troubles, often relegated to simply a Northern Irish issue, did not directly contribute to the rise of far-right xenophobia in the Republic of Ireland. However, the moderation of Sinn Féin following the Good Friday Agreement did lead to the political isolation of its traditionally radical workingclass base. This disaffection, when combined with contemporary socioeconomic pressures, generated conditions in which far-right actors were able to mobilize support. By identifying this mechanism, the study hopes to provide a foundation for further research in both Irish politics and historical examinations of the effects of the Troubles.

title: Residents’ Right to the City in Barcelona, Venice, and Seoul
abstract: This paper expands on the existing research and contributes more robust findings by investigating the gendered effects of austerity policy across countries and time. I answer the following question: “Do austerity policies disproportionately affect women?” In my exploration of this question, I consider social and political factors that may be influential. First I explain relevant findings in the literature. Next, I lay out my hypotheses which predict that austerity, or some elements of it, disproportionately limit women’s ability to pursue economic success. To evaluate my hypotheses, I employ a time-series cross-section regression to evaluate the relationship between fiscal adjustment and changes in gender inequality indicators across countries and over time. I find that there is a lack of a strong relationship between the economic gender gap and austerity measures. It is important to evaluate systems that support or exacerbate inequality, and this paper aims to do just that.

title: Revisiting Mendelberg: Implicitness, Explicitness, and the Racial Politics of Messenger Identity
abstract: Scholars have long argued that the “norm of racial equality” constrains explicit racial rhetoric, leading political actors to rely on implicit appeals to avoid electoral sanction (Mendelberg 2001). This study reexamines that framework in a contemporary context marked by the increased visibility of explicit racial discourse. I hypothesize that explicit racial rhetoric will generate greater candidate sanctioning than implicit appeals, that White candidates will be sanctioned more than Black candidates for delivering racialized messages, and that racial resentment will reduce sanctioning among high-resentment individuals. To test these expectations, I conduct a preregistered survey experiment in which White respondents evaluate political candidates across variations in rhetoric type and candidate race in two policy domains. The results provide limited support for the expectation that explicit rhetoric produces greater sanctioning and only modest evidence that White candidates are penalized more than Black candidates. In contrast, racial resentment emerges as a strong and consistent predictor of candidate evaluation, with higher-resentment individuals significantly less likely to impose sanctions. These findings suggest that racial norms continue to shape political judgment but are unevenly enforced and increasingly dependent on individual attitudes.

title: Framing the American Dream: Race, Merit, and Inequality in U.S. Billionaire Discourse
abstract: Economic inequality in the United States has reached historic levels, yet public faith in meritocracy and the American Dream remains remarkably durable. How do the wealthiest Americans themselves explain this inequality — and what do they choose not to say? This thesis develops a replicable coding framework to systematically analyze public-facing discourse from the top 100 U.S. billionaires (Forbes 2025), drawing on interviews, speeches, shareholder letters, and philanthropic communications. Organizing discourse along two core dimensions — meritocratic versus structural accounts of inequality and color-evasive versus race-conscious racial framing — I code 159 documents across 25 individuals. I find that the modal pattern of billionaire discourse is Meritocratic and Color-Evasive: elites consistently attribute success to individual effort, innovation, and resilience while almost entirely avoiding explicit engagement with race. Race appears in only 13% of coded documents. More striking is the prevalence of conflicting frames — structural diagnosis paired with individual or philanthropic prescription — appearing in 51% of documents, suggesting that elite legitimation operates not through simple denial of inequality but through strategic acknowledgment that stops short of structural remedy. Together, these patterns reveal how economic elites construct and sustain narratives that make extreme wealth appear earned, natural, and inevitable in a multiracial democracy.

title: Performative Activism on College Campuses: An Investigation into Efficacy
abstract: Performative activism is prevalent in the undergraduate student ecosystem. Defined as activism without intentions outside of oneself, performative activism is understudied in its impact on social movements and their success. This thesis asks: Does performative activism minimize effective activism practices on college campuses, and can the drawbacks of performative activism be minimized? Through survey experiments and interviews, I discover that altogether, college students do not believe that either social media or land acknowledgments are effective modes of activism, regardless of individual participant exposure.

title: Justifying the Means: Explaining Generational Differences in Support for Political Violence
abstract: Political violence is on the rise in the United States. A string of high-profile assassinations and attempts in the last two years prompted a vast array of reactions. After the murder of right-wing activist Charlie Kirk, polling data revealed a large generational gap in support for political violence, with Generation Z being much more willing to justify its use than older Americans. This thesis seeks to explain why. Using an original survey experiment, I find that younger Americans’ increased support for political violence is explained by their stronger anti-establishment attitudes and, to a lesser extent, their Democratic partisanship. Older Americans, who have more faith in American democracy, are consequently less likely to support acts of political violence.

title: Art and the Adversary: American Audience Perceptions of Russian Opera Amid the Russo-Ukrainian War
abstract: This thesis examines how exposure to information about the Russo-Ukrainian War and a given performer’s political stance shapes American audience perceptions of Russian opera. Using a 2×3 factorial experimental design administered to 630 participants after screening via Prolific and Qualtrics, the study randomly assigns participants to one of two priming conditions (war-primed or unprimed) and one of three performer-information conditions (anti-war, pro-war, or no information) before they view a roughly 90-second clip of Tatyana’s Letter Scene from Tchaikovsky’s Eugene Onegin, performed by soprano Anna Netrebko. Five dependent variables capture audience perceptions: perceived political alignment, emotional response, support for programming, aesthetic perception, and moral acceptability. Drawing on priming theory, soft power, and Social Identity Theory, this study fills a notable gap in the literature by empirically testing how political context conditions audience reception of performing arts during an active international conflict, particularly after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. OLS regression models are used to estimate the independent and interactive effects of the two treatment variables on each outcome measure. Results indicate that political information about the performer, particularly the pro-war condition, exerts a stronger influence on audience perceptions than war priming alone, with notable effects on moral acceptability and support for programming. These findings carry implications for cultural institutions navigating programming decisions, for larger academic scholarship on the political dimensions of the consumption of live performance, and for broader understandings of cultural diplomacy during wartime.

title: Institutionalizing Inequality: Democracy and the Persistence of Wealth Inequality in Chile and Ecuador
abstract: Latin America is simultaneously the most unequal and most democratic region in the developing world, yet standard theory predicts that democracy should reduce inequality over time. This study confronts that paradox through a comparative analysis of Chile and Ecuador, two countries that, despite dramatically different institutional trajectories, both erupted in mass protest against their democratically elected governments in October 2019. Chile, celebrated as one of the region’s most stable liberal democracies, holds nearly double the wealth concentration of Ecuador, a country defined by chronic institutional instability. If democracy is supposed to empower majorities to demand redistribution, why does the democratic success story exhibit higher inequality than the country that does not? Employing qualitative historical process tracing from each country’s democratization period through the early 2020s, this study analyzes constitutional design, party system institutionalization, judicial independence, and tax structures to trace how inequality becomes self-reinforcing within democratic systems. The analysis finds that both countries are caught in inequality traps, but through fundamentally different mechanisms. Chile represents an ‘elite-biased democracy,’ in which wealthy interests are embedded within formal institutional frameworks. Ecuador represents a ‘captured democracy’ where elites sustain inequality through more visible methods including corruption and judicial manipulation. This framework challenges the assumption that strong liberal institutions improve conditions for reducing inequality. Instead, institutional design and who those institutions protect matters deeply. Democratic institutions alone cannot dismantle entrenched wealth concentration—and may even preserve it in a more stable way..

title: Beyond the Model Minority: Explaining Asian American Political Engagement Through Contact, Memory, and Civic Organizations
abstract: This thesis examines the conditions under which Asian Americans engage in minority coalition building and achieve meaningful political incorporation through a comparative analysis of Monterey Park, Oakland, and Irvine. It argues that due to Asian Americans’ structurally ambivalent position within the U.S. racial hierarchy, explaining variation in their political incorporation requires moving beyond socioeconomic status to examine three contextual mechanisms: intergroup contact, collective memory of racial discrimination, and the presence of inclusive civic organizations. Using a mixed methods approach, the study integrates precinct level electoral analysis of the 2024 presidential election, qualitative archival research on community responses to the Black Lives Matter and Stop Asian Hate movements, and civic opportunity data. The findings show that intergroup contact is associated with stronger electoral coalition building with other racial minority groups at the aggregate level, but weakens substantially within Asian American homogeneous precincts. Collective memory of racial discrimination emerges as a more consistent driver of cross racial political mobilization, although its effects depend on the nature of the discrimination experienced. Most importantly, this study concludes that Asian American political incorporation hinges on the presence of inclusive civic organizations that can convert intergroup contact and shared experiences of discrimination into sustained cross racial coalition building.

title: Coercion in the commons: Private university administrations’ responses to graduate worker unionization 2016-2025
abstract: Graduate worker unions are one of the fastest-growing sectors of the labor movement. Since 2016, the number of graduate worker unions has nearly tripled. However, given their unique circumstance as both students and workers, graduate workers have been largely excluded from studies on managerial responses to union campaigns. Through a descriptive inference approach using case studies of five private universities—Columbia, Harvard, Northwestern, Duke, and Princeton—researchers determined the most common methods university administrations use to respond to graduate workers unionization campaigns. The primary data set was created by conducting interviews with graduate worker organizers from each university. Using these interviews, supplemented with news articles, NLRB findings, and relevant webpages, researchers coded individual instances in which universities responded to an aspect of the graduate worker union campaign into larger categories. The most common categories include delaying bargaining sessions, limiting the bargaining unit, promoting anti-union messaging, and hiring an anti-union law firm. These are the same tactics used by managers in non-university sectors, although university administrations tailored them to their unique environment. Understanding these strategies provides critical insight not only into the future of labor organizing in higher education, but also into broader patterns of employer response across emerging sectors of the labor movement.

title: Coercion or Cooperation: American Security Force Assistance in an Era of Great Power Competition
abstract: One way the United States expresses its power is through providing Security Force Assistance (SFA) to partner nations; however, the character of SFA must adapt over time. Since the beginning of the Global War on Terror SFA has focused on counterinsurgency operations. Today, the reestablishment of great power competition changes the focus of SFA, necessitating a change in U.S. policy. By exploring the cases of Ukraine, Taiwan, and South Korea, this study will examine the effects of four main variables on a country expecting war’s embracement of American SFA: (1) its attitude towards military sovereignty, (2) its threat proximity, (3) its historical relations with the U.S., and (4) its economic integration with the United States. These four factors provide insight into the effectiveness of SFA, providing lessons on how the U.S. can better structure SFA in a manner better adapted for the geopolitical environment of today.

title: Meaningless Buzzword or Moral Call to Action? The Effect of the Term Genocide on Ukrainians’ Levels of Political Engagement Explored through Ethnic Identification
abstract: Governments and NGO advocacy groups have long considered the word “genocide” a catalyst for action, believing classifying an atrocity as such leads to increased public pressure to intervene. With debates currently raging around the globe as to what conflicts constitute a genocide, it is critical to understand how terminology can influence public support for intervention, which in turn may affect foreign policy decisions. Using Ukraine as a case study, this work utilizes a survey experiment to better understand how genocide, as opposed to the more general term war, impacts the political engagement and priorities of ethnic Ukrainians born in Ukraine as well as those born in the United States. This relationship is further explored through an additional analysis of respondents’ levels of ethnic identification. Going against popular belief, the results of this study suggest that the term genocide does not lead to significant shifts in political engagement or policy priorities, showing that the social power of the word does not always translate into political action. Results also found that genocide decreases levels of ethnic identification for ethnic Ukrainians born in the United States, while having no effect on the other respondent groups. These findings further suggest that the term genocide can be used according to its intended legal purpose by governments without a corresponding outcry from the public.

title: Shaping Success or Stifling Potential? Examining The Relationship Between Academic Achievement and Exclusionary Discipline in Chicago Public and Charter Schools
abstract: As the charter school movement continues to expand and education reform remains a salient issue in American politics, it is essential to understand what factors impact student performance. Exclusionary discipline has been widely regarded as a major inhibitor of student success. This study explores that relationship by utilizing aggregate data on discipline rates, SAT scores, graduation rates, and college enrollment rates to investigate whether charter schools use disciplinary action at a disproportionate rate and determine if disciplinary action affects academic achievement. While the results from this study were not statistically significant, the findings align with previous research that suggests a negative correlation between suspensions and academic performance.

title: Race-ing for Success A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Racial Inequality in NCAA DI Women’s Cross Country Running
abstract: Despite the success of many non-White international distance runners, non-White American women are disproportionately underrepresented amongst NCAA DI Women’s Cross Country (WCC) participants and top performers. This study aims to analyze the causal pathways and institutions that result in the outsourcing of talent, rather than investment in non-White American women. To determine whether there is a causal relationship between race and success of NCAA DI WCC athletes, this study utilizes mixed-methods research with a Critical Race Theory foundation. Quantitative research analyzed the race and nationality of top-ten finishers at the NCAA DI WCC Championships from 2015-2024. Qualitative research was conducted using thematic analysis of survey responses from current B1G Conference WCC student-athletes. Survey questions aimed to seek a detailed understanding of the processes that lead to participation and success in women’s distance running, as well as what role, if any, race plays in athletic success. This study finds that non-White American women are overwhelmingly underrepresented among top-ten NCAA DI WCC Championship finishers, and that A Sense of Belonging, Opportunity, and Community were important thematic factors contributing to B1G athletes’ participation and success in WCC.

title: Navigating the Information Age: How a Saturated Media Environment Affects Political Knowledge
abstract: With the rise of the internet, cable news, and social media, the availability of political news is greater than ever before. An informed electorate is essential for a functioning democracy, making it crucial to understand how the modern high-choice news landscape influences knowledge. The vast increase in available information has raised concerns about potential information overload and its role in widening the political knowledge gap across different education levels and content preferences. However, there is a gap in the literature regarding the causal, short-term effects of the volume of sources on knowledge acquisition. This study addresses that gap through a causal experiment, examining how the availability of multiple sources affects knowledge gain on a specific topic in a short time-frame. The results indicate a causal link in which increasing the number of sources available increases knowledge gain on the topic. The effect was not impacted by the education level or political interest of participants. These findings challenge prior assumptions and suggest the need for further research into the mechanisms driving knowledge acquisition in a high-choice media environment.

title: "We are the union”: a case study of a local union's internal structure
Manipulated Maps, Manipulated Participation: How Partisan Gerrymandering Influences Conventional and Unconventional Political Engagement
abstract: Partisan gerrymandering poses a unique challenge to the American political system. Defined as the process of redistricting legislative districts to give one party an outsized advantage, partisan gerrymandering causes disadvantaged parties to lose meaningful representation in Congress. What is unknown is how changes in representation due to gerrymandering affect participation. This thesis answers the question: “What is the effect of partisan gerrymandering on conventional and unconventional forms of participation?” Using data from the Cooperative Election Study (CES) and a unique survey experiment, I find that Americans do not modify participation levels based on simply living in a gerrymandered district. On the contrary, when individuals are primed to think about the effects of gerrymandering within their district, they are more willing to unconventionally participate in the future. Similarly, when individuals are primed to think about not being gerrymandered, they are more willing to conventionally participate.

title: Protest Participation Through the Lens of Grievance Theory: How Economic Factors and Individuals’ Perceptions of Conditions Shape Significant Anti-Government Protests From 2017 to 2023
abstract: This study examines how macroeconomic factors and individuals’ perceptions of conditions influence protest participation from 2017 to 2023, with a focus on how these factors shape protests motivated by economic versus non-economic grievances. Grounded in Grievance Theory, which posits that economic hardship fuels political unrest by heightening perceptions of injustice, it employs cross-national economic and survey data to assess both objective and subjective economic factors. The objective analysis examines how unemployment, income per capita, income growth, income disparities, and fiscal policy ratings correlate with protest participation. The subjective analysis explores the role of perceived relative economic deprivation, financial insecurity, and government accountability in shaping individuals’ likelihood of protesting. The findings suggest that while macroeconomic indicators show weak correlations with protest participation, subjective perceptions are significantly more predictive. This highlights the role of perceived injustice in mobilization, reinforcing that economic conditions alone may be insufficient to drive protest participation.

title: Reducing Affective Polarization: Is Proportional Representation the Answer?
abstract: Affective polarization threatens democratic governance around the world, and it is paramount that solutions be found to reduce this phenomenon. The emerging comparative literature on affective polarization has found some evidence of a relationship between proportional representation (PR) electoral systems and reduced affective polarization. However, methodological limitations of existing work (which primarily relies on OLS regression analyses) make it unclear if this relationship is causal. To provide better insight into the nature of this relationship, this study uses an alternative method: difference-in-differences (DID) with Mahalanobis distance matching. This method is also used to provide an initial assessment of three potential intervening variables (or mechanisms) that could connect electoral system to affective polarization: satisfaction with democracy, economic inequality, and representation of disadvantaged groups. This study finds no statistically significant relationship between electoral system and affective polarization, as well as no significant relationship between electoral system and two of the possible intervening variables (economic inequality and representation of disadvantaged groups), casting doubt on their ability to actually serve as intervening variables. Insufficient data prevented the testing of the relationship between electoral system and satisfaction with democracy. This study’s findings suggest that there may not be a strong causal relationship between electoral system and affective polarization. Therefore, we must exercise caution when recommending electoral system change as a solution to affective polarization.

title: From Expansion to Equity: Leveraging Telehealth to Mitigate Healthcare Disparities During and Beyond the COVID-19 Pandemic
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic precipitated a worldwide health emergency, laying bare the underlying systemic weaknesses and necessitating immediate structural reforms in healthcare provisioning. Telehealth became a critical response, utilizing information and communication technologies to maintain continuity of care, improve infection control, and reduce workforce shortages. This study evaluates the pandemic's growth of telehealth on access to healthcare, patient engagement, and public trust, particularly in older and rural patients with digital literacy issues, broadband limitations, and regulatory barriers. Through the comparison and contrast of South Korea's centralized system and the United States decentralized model, this research employs a mixed-methods approach—quantitative analysis using R to quantify outcomes on health and qualitative analysis of policy to assess government transparency and individuals' trust of telehealth systems. The results determine structural discrepancies in telehealth utilization and emphasize the necessity for fair and sustainable digital health policies for long-term healthcare resilience.

title: Austerity and the Economic Gender Gap
abstract: This paper expands on the existing research and contributes more robust findings by investigating the gendered effects of austerity policy across countries and time. I answer the following question: “Do austerity policies disproportionately affect women?” In my exploration of this question, I consider social and political factors that may be influential. First I explain relevant findings in the literature. Next, I lay out my hypotheses which predict that austerity, or some elements of it, disproportionately limit women’s ability to pursue economic success. To evaluate my hypotheses, I employ a time-series cross-section regression to evaluate the relationship between fiscal adjustment and changes in gender inequality indicators across countries and over time. I find that there is a lack of a strong relationship between the economic gender gap and austerity measures. It is important to evaluate systems that support or exacerbate inequality, and this paper aims to do just that.

title: An Independence Movement "Left" behind by the Right: The Far-Right's Growth in the Context of the Catalan Independence Referendum
abstract: An increase in nationalism and the birth of far-right movements have swept across continental Europe over the last decade, with scholars highlighting parallels between many of the platforms of these far-right parties. Many of which are built upon anti-immigration, anti-LGBTQ, and anti-abortion stances. Interestingly, the birth of the far-right in Catalonia is in the context of a unique political situation, the Catalan Independence Referendum of 2017. This leads to the possibility of a new factor that could have shaped far-right party support and preferences on Catalan independence. Using graphical analysis and linear regressions to examine Catalan opinion polls from 2014 through 2024, this work investigates what factors led to the rise of the far-right, whether Catalan independence stances or more widespread far-right ideologies. This work concludes that even though there are far-right links to Spanish identity and institutional discontent, reactions against the independence movement and a consistent belief in the regional integration of Catalonia drove this growth. These conclusions illustrate the difficulty the independence movement in Catalonia will face in the future, given a decrease in Catalan identity and support for independence in the context of Vox’s emergence.

title: All or Nothing: Exploring Asymmetric Information and Resource Sustainability
abstract: This thesis investigates how various asymmetric information structures impact cooperation and strategy in communal resource-sharing situations. 176 participants played a resource distribution game, with varying amounts of information. Findings suggest that total visibility or complete lack thereof fosters optimal cooperation, while partial information leads to suboptimal, unsustainable outcomes. Specifically, free-rider behavior is observed in scenarios where participants believe other players are colluding without them, leading to increased token extraction. These findings suggest that half-hearted coordination efforts may be less effective than no coordination at all, highlighting the importance of comprehensive and committed collective action. By understanding these underlying mechanisms, researchers can gain valuable insights into how to design more effective conservation initiatives.

title: Disorderly Discourse: Analyzing the Internal Disunity of Russia’s Liberal Opposition
abstract: Russia’s liberal opposition, especially in recent years, has consistently struggled with the issue of unification despite the wide variety of leaders and movements that oppose President Putin. This problem remains important to investigate given that prior research on other nations has suggested that opposition unity is a necessary factor in the replacement/overthrowing of authoritarian regimes. With this in mind, I have posed the following question for my research: What factors prevent Russia's liberal opposition from successfully unifying and mounting successful action against President Putin, especially following the events of 2022? To answer this question, I have looked into the positions of four opposition leaders and their respective movements – Alexei Navalny, Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Garry Kasparov, and Maxim Katz – to determine whether contentions preventing unification arise from ideological policy, tactical, or personality differences. My research has shown that out of these three categories, personality differences have been shown to cause the most issues between the leaders, and even their supporters, with ideological policy being the least contentious factor. Such a conclusion poses multiple questions, specifically surrounding the viability of the liberal opposition’s continued operation given that its leadership repeatedly makes an effort to consolidate power around themselves, and does not shy away from public accusations and insults. Following the death of Alexei Navalny, a moment some thought could lead to some mending of relations, the personal attacks have only increased, with leaders and supporters alike being arguably in a more divided state than before. Just two months later, the opposition has seemed to largely have moved on from him despite efforts of the Anti-Corruption Foundation to establish his name as a symbol of anti-government resistance – an effort largely considered a failure by other leaders. Navalny’s passing combined with the sheer amount of ongoing personal attacks and contentions amongst liberal leadership ultimately suggest an uncertain future for Russia’s liberal opposition, at least, in the form it exists today.

title: Redesigning the Filibuster for More Effective Lawmaking in a Polarized Senate
abstract: In today’s hyper-partisan political environment, it is a common complaint that Congress is broken. This is especially true for the Senate, where the filibuster and cloture rule have created a de facto requirement for a 60-vote supermajority to pass almost any legislation, sparking widespread calls from activists and senators alike to reform or even abolish the filibuster. In this paper, I predict the effects of different proposals for the filibuster and cloture rule on a set of “legislative goods,” including productivity, bipartisanship, and policy stability. I test the effects of three different filibuster rule proposals on these legislative goods. To predict the effects of these rule changes, I extend Wawro and Schickler’s expected-utility model of legislative entrepreneurship under cloture by considering the costs faced by bill proponents and obstructionists alike. Using this model, which excels at explaining the evolution of past filibuster fights, I predict the outcomes of legislative battles under different filibuster rules. The results will inform activists and senators in future debates over filibuster reform — which will inevitably return the next time a popular bill is stymied by the Senate’s supermajoritarian rules.

title: Investigating the Effects of Populist Rhetoric on Confidence in Representative Democracy in the United States
abstract: As the salience of populist political movements grows across the Western world, so has the body of research and discourse that considers what threat, if any, populism could pose to the stability of democratic institutions. This is in part due to the anti-establishment rhetoric that characterizes populism, as it rejects the capabilities of representative institutions to represent and respond to the people, functions which are fundamental to American democracy. The objective of this study is to provide insights into whether exposure to the rhetoric that populists employ has the ability to weaken the American peoples’ confidence in representative institutions, both in their effectiveness in representing and serving the interests of the public they are elected to represent, and in their stability. This relationship is investigated using a survey experiment, in which participants are randomly exposed to either neutral or populist messaging from a candidate running to be the president of the United States. Findings suggest that exposure to populist rhetoric did in fact reduce confidence in the efficacy of institutions.

title: The Birds, The Bees, and The Bureaucracy: A Cross-National Analysis of Abortion Policy Determinants
abstract: Few issues in modern political discourse are more controversial than abortion. As such, abortion policies vary greatly from country to country, with some countries prohibiting the procedure altogether while others permit abortion “on demand.” Given that the safety of abortion procedures diverges widely between countries with liberal abortion policies and those with more restrictive ones, cross-national variation in abortion policies has important implications for international public health and gender equality. To shed light on the reasons for cross-country differences in abortion policies, this study uses bivariate and multivariate analyses to determine how ten independent variables correlate with abortion policy outcomes in 187 countries. The results suggest that Human Development Index, Gender Development Index, women’s representation in parliament, earlier allowance of women’s suffrage, women’s representation in the labor force, women’s educational attainment, gross domestic product per capita, and gross national income per capita are all positively correlated with liberal national abortion policies, while Gender Inequality Index and religiosity are negatively correlated with liberal abortion policies.

title: Corporate America Under Siege: The Electoral Effects of Political Attacks on Private Enterprise
abstract: There are countless examples, both past and present, of U.S. politicians harshly criticizing corporations and using the powers of their office to, at times, inhibit a business’s ability to generate revenue and profit. Moments of tension between government and businesses should be expected given the government’s mostly regulatory and oversight role with respect to private markets. However, recently, there appears to be a new highly adversarial relationship forming between select businesses and politicians. A growing number of corporations across the U.S. have begun openly and intentionally delving into the political arena exercising their right to free speech to criticize policies and politicians. In response to corporations becoming perhaps more open in their opposition, or support of political policies, especially highly contentious ones, certain politicians have begun implementing an incipient political tactic: vindictively, loudly, and harshly attacking businesses to hurt their profit-making ability and push them into silence. This thesis uses an experiment to answer whether voters support this emerging political tactic, and under what circumstances their support might increase or wane. Results from my experiment reveal that partisanship, specifically whether the voter shares the party of the “attacker politician,” is the biggest predictor determining whether a voter will even consider supporting these types of attacks. Further, even when these attacks are initiated by an in-party politician (same party affiliation as the respondent), there is no evidence to suggest that the politician benefits electorally from engaging in the attack. Harsh attacks against a business, however, including those initiated by an in-party politician, were emphatically rejected by voters. Overall, politicians stand to gain very little from their own party by engaging in these types of attacks, and risk losing even greater support from voters of the opposite party.

title: How the Presence of Syrian Refugees Affects Elections in Turkey
abstract: The 2023 elections in Turkey brought negative national sentiment towards Syrian refugees to the fore in both campaign messaging and public opinion polls. This thesis explores how the presence of refugees affected the 2023 presidential and parliamentary elections in Turkey and the mechanisms and theories that shape this relationship. The following research assesses the impact of the presence of Syrian refugees on voting for the 2023 presidential and parliamentary elections through a mixed methods approach consisting of regional voting, survey data and Geographic Information Systems (GIS) analyses. In the presidential elections, the results indicated that the presence of refugees did not have a statistically significant effect on voting for the anti-refugee candidate, Kemal Kilicdaroglu. Conversely, in the parliamentary elections, the results suggest that a higher concentration of refugees in a province, particularly in major metropolitan centers, correlates with increased support for extreme single-issue antirefugee parties, exemplified by the findings for the Zafer Party. The research also considers how the mechanisms of intergroup contact between Syrian refugees and Turks impacts voting for anti-refugee parties and finds that contact may lead to a slight increase in support for anti-refugee candidates. These findings underscore the importance of single-issue anti-refugee parties in the nexus between the presence of refugees and electoral outcomes in host countries.

title: War and Politics After Fifty Years: the Vietnam War and Vietnamese American Political Preferences on Immigration
abstract: Out of all of the Asian ethnic groups in the United States, Vietnamese Americans tend to hold conservative political preferences, including on the issue of immigration. This paper aimed to understand how the Vietnam War and the experiences and historical memories of this era translate into political preferences on immigration, and what variables might cause any differences in political preferences among Vietnamese Americans. Primarily through qualitative interviews, this paper sought to confirm whether there was a relationship between the Vietnam War and political preferences on immigration at all, and if immigrant generation might be a variable in discerning any differences within the community. What was eventually discovered was that there is a direct relationship between the Vietnam War and the years that followed (immigration and the process of resettlement) and political preferences on immigration. With this relationship supported by the interviews, it was also concluded that political preferences on immigration were varied by immigrant generation, age, and nativity, based on the different experiences faced by these different demographics. It was the personal experiences of each ,individual that seemed to determine political preferences on immigration rather than any other variables. This research helps better understand political preferences within the Vietnamese American community, and perhaps the understanding of political preferences overall.

title: Correcting Republican Misperceptions of a Socialist Threat
abstract: Prior research has established that part of the anti-democratic sentiment seen from American partisans stems from perceptions that rival partisans are more anti-democratic than they truly are. A common way to combat this is to correct partisans with real data from out-partisans and measure the resulting change in anti-democratic sentiment. This study examines whether American Republicans’ view of socialism as anti-democratic and popular among Democrats may exacerbate their anti-democratic sentiments. To explore such perceptions, an initial survey with 720 partisans (split evenly between parties) was conducted followed by a preregistered survey experiment with 1,396 Republicans who were corrected with true Democratic support for socialism. This research finds that although Republicans view socialism through an anti-democratic lens, a correction with real-world data is an ineffective strategy in decreasing anti-democratic sentiment. Furthermore, I uncover evidence that Republicans are strikingly accurate when assessing Democratic support of socialism and that greater estimates of Democratic support are associated with increases in their own anti-democratic sentiment.

title: Machine Learning Analysis of COVID-19: Exploring Determinants of Spread, Mortality, and Governance Responses
abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic necessitated immediate and strategic interventions from global governments to minimize its adverse effects on public health, economic stability, and societal norms. This paper assesses the key challenges faced by researchers and addresses factor selection problems. It critically assesses traditional correlational studies and parametric analyses. The paper advances current methodologies in handling extensive, cross-sectional datasets with machine learning approaches - using LASSO regression and the Random Forest algorithm combined with various imputation methods to analyze 1,685 potential factors in 172 countries. The paper offers a roadmap for conducting inductive machine learning. This is particularly useful for empirical studies where primary subjects are abstract across different fields. By evaluating over a thousand potential variables, the study identifies critical predictors of pandemic severity and effective governmental responses. The paper discusses long-term strategies for enhancing societal resilience against global health crises, expanding the research frontier by introducing novel hypotheses about governance and institutional structures.
